line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 c3 Nf6 e5
teaches: A central pawn push made before you can support it just loses time — when the advance can be met by a clean capture that leaves you ahead in development, welcome it. The space it grabbed evaporates and you are simply better for having let it come.
explains: The pawn to e5 attacks the knight on f6 and looks aggressive — but it is premature. The pawn on c3 is sitting idle, the e5-pawn itself has no proper support, so we just take it. Grab it and Black comes out a full tempo ahead in development.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 c3 Nf6 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Nbd7
teaches: Meet a centralised enemy knight by challenging it with a developing move that offers a trade on your terms — bringing a piece out while forcing the exchange beats tolerating the knight in your camp.
explains: Rather than let the knight sit proudly on e5, the knight to d7 develops and attacks it, offering the swap. Whatever White chooses, Black comes out comfortably developed and a shade better — the intruder is challenged the moment it lands.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 c3 Nf6 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Nbd7 Nxd7 Bxd7
teaches: When you recapture, do it with the piece that also develops — a recapture that brings a man toward activity is two moves in one. Prefer the take that improves your position over the passive one.
explains: You could take back with the queen — but the bishop is better. Recapturing with it develops the piece and sets up a reroute to c6 on the long diagonal. The same capture, but it brings a man into the game instead of just restoring the count.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 c3 Nf6 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Nbd7 Nxd7 Bxd7 Bc4 Bc6
teaches: An awkwardly placed bishop should be rerouted to its best diagonal, and doing it with a gain of tempo forces the opponent to react before you finish your own plan — move the bad piece to a good square while attacking something.
explains: The bishop swings to c6, seizing the long diagonal and hitting the g2-pawn, so White has to stop and deal with it. That bought tempo lets Black calmly finish with e6, the dark-squared bishop and castling — the bad piece is now the good one, and for free.
